pointers.locator: Section IIA, discussion after Assumptions 2 and 3
pointers.statement: The paper situates its own instrument within a taxonomy it builds from the prior literature, listing several well-known instruments as examples of plausibly hidden instruments and others as examples of plausibly transparent instruments.
A dynamic siting model of a planner versus a delegated local policymaker is developed first and yields four numbered predictions that the empirical section later maps results onto one by one.

A cheap-talk model yields four numbered implications (belief updating, heterogeneity by preference gap, fertility, transfers) and each empirical subsection is introduced as a test of a named implication.

The approach is named as a multi-discontinuity extension of the standard bunching estimator, distinguishing threshold-specific observed elasticities from structural parameters recovered by pooling many bunching observations in one regression.

Replicating the gradient across districts within provinces is presented as a test of the policy interpretation: centrally planned, top-down policies should produce the same pattern at each administrative level, so within-province estimates with province-year fixed effects are used as corroborating d
The design variant is named as Neyman-orthogonal moment-condition estimation with cross-fitting, built on doubly robust efficient scores drawn from the prior semiparametric efficiency literature.

The authors discuss the political-economy origins of within-occupation interstate policy variation, admit they do not fully understand them, and point to appendix tests using partisan self-identification data.
The authors report verifying their interpretation of the advisor's policy directly with the institution and cite conversations for how the policy originated.

pointers.locator: Section II.C, referencing Online Appendix A.3
pointers.statement: Reports a quantitative exogenous-timing check: state-year unemployment, partisan composition, school resources, and evolution/creationism search intensity are regressed on the evolution score with state and year fixed effects, with the coefficients detailed in the Online Appendix.

pointers.locator: Introduction, paragraph on the teaching occupation
pointers.statement: The authors frame the study population as facing low adjustment barriers and label the context a proof of concept for the role of information constraints, setting reader expectations about scope before results are shown.
The event-study regression controls for the running variable within the narrow band and is described as functionally similar to an RD design.

The reduced-form demand equation used in the empirical section is asserted in footnotes to be the same as the demand function later derived from the model, and the derived elasticities are discussed as special cases of a more general specification with imperfect substitutes.

Explicitly explains why a regression discontinuity design is not used for the administration reform: the exact assignment formula is unknown and no sharp discontinuity in assignment probability is observed in the data.
The paper explicitly contrasts its coverage results with impossibility theorems in the literature and states why it does not describe its own results as impossibility results.

pointers.locator: Introduction (setting paragraph) and Section IV.E Empirical Strategy, equation (1)
pointers.statement: The estimating equation is displayed once, numbered (1), with separate indicators for treated and spillover individuals, individual and school-level controls and stratification fixed effects; the same equation is referenced in every table note. The Monte Carlo design is fully enumerated: baseline model, three numbered regressor designs, two numbered error designs, the grid of cluster counts, and homogeneous cluster size, with citations explaining why particular designs produce high leverage.

Identification of bunching itself rests on an explicitly stated assumption that the retirement-age density would have been smooth absent the threshold, noted before the excess-mass formula is derived.

The ATE regression is presented with two named assumptions, parallel trends (tested later via event-time indicators) and SUTVA; spillovers to control firms are argued to bias toward underestimating the effect.

The contribution is framed as a theoretical case built on two insights (variance bias and interval coverage), and the scope condition that both results assume correct specification is stated up front in the introduction.

A stylized intertemporal choice model with durable/tradable goods yields three propositions that map one-to-one onto the outcome columns of the main table; proofs are relegated to an appendix and a CRRA extension to the Internet Appendix.

The estimator is rewritten as a weighted average of heterogeneous cell-level effects following de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille; the share of negative weights is reported in a footnote and an appendix table ranks occupations by weight. The authors state what homogeneity is required (within occupa

pointers.locator: Introduction; Section III, Intervention and timetable
pointers.statement: Names the intervention as a two-sided information design in which consumers receive the price-transparency and/or monitoring information and vendors are separately told their customers received it, distinguishing it from one-sided disclosure experiments.

pointers.locator: Section 4, definition of F and F*, Theorem 2
pointers.statement: Bias and coverage results are stated as infima over explicitly defined model classes (all designs satisfying the assumptions, and a subclass with clusterwise invertibility), holding the number of regressors and clusters fixed while cluster sizes, regressors and covariance matrices vary freely.
Reports a manipulation test on the density of the running variable at the cutoff, presented together with a companion density figure in the main text.

The comparison of subgroup treatment-effect differences estimated in-sample versus in a held-out sample is used as the paper's central diagnostic for whether the predicted heterogeneity reflects a genuine pattern rather than overfitting.

The note's only formal validity check for the estimator is a theorem establishing uniform asymptotic normality and confidence-interval coverage over a class of data-generating processes satisfying the stated conditions, rather than an empirical diagnostic table.
Uses a policy subperiod during which the schedule kink was removed as a placebo test of the regression kink design, estimating the change in slope in that subperiod.

A dedicated balance table regresses predetermined appellant characteristics on case outcome and separately on the leniency instrument, reporting a joint test of whether those characteristics predict judge leniency as evidence for random assignment.

A balance table comparing respondent characteristics across the control and treatment arms of the main experiment is placed in the main text immediately before the headline results, its purpose stated as confirming that randomization succeeded.

pointers.locator: Section II, closing paragraph before Section III
pointers.statement: The proof of the main theorem is not given in the printed note but is stated to be deferred to an online appendix relying on a Chebyshev-inequality and central-limit-theorem argument.

pointers.locator: Section IIIA, referencing online Appendix Figure B-4
pointers.statement: Reports a density-continuity test in the spirit of a standard manipulation test for the running variable around the kink threshold, checking continuity of the wage density and its first derivative, with the test itself placed in an online appendix.

pointers.locator: Section IIIB, online Appendix Table A3
pointers.statement: Monotonicity is probed indirectly by checking that subgroup-specific first stages are never negative and by re-estimating the leniency instrument on complementary subpopulations, with the underlying estimates placed in an online appendix table and only the qualitative conclusion discussed in the mai

pointers.locator: Section III.A, referencing Appendix Figure B2
pointers.statement: A manipulation test on the running variable's density, using the number of properties across the boundary, is run and reported in an appendix figure.

A placebo diagnostic randomly reassigns antenna locations across many simulated draws and re-estimates the benchmark model; the main text summarizes an average null finding across the simulations while the full simulation results are reported only in an online appendix table.

States that the same negative-weight and sensitivity diagnostics computed for the two applications are recommended more generally to practitioners as a first step before deciding whether to compute the new estimator.

Presents a graphical balance check plotting individual characteristics such as age and region of origin against the running variable, arguing visually that these covariates move smoothly through the cutoff rather than jumping.

pointers.locator: Section IIIA, referencing online Appendix Figure B-5
pointers.statement: Checks smoothness of observable worker characteristics as a function of wage around the kink threshold, treating non-smoothness in observables as evidence against the identifying assumption on unobserved heterogeneity.

A dedicated balance table reports RD coefficients for a wide set of pre-treatment property, sewer-access, and amenity-distance variables, offered as evidence on continuity at the boundary.

An indirect exogeneity check tests whether pre-existing household characteristics from a household survey predict the future intensity of messaging in a village, functioning as a balance-style diagnostic but described only in a footnote.

pointers.locator: footnote 26; online Appendix Figure B3 (not available)
pointers.statement: A placebo check on a filler question about the minimum wage, unrelated to the gender-norm treatment, is reported in an online appendix figure and described in the main text as showing no treatment effect, supporting the claim that the intervention updated norm-specific beliefs rather than beliefs in

Pre-epidemic rental prices and pre-epidemic cholera-exposure proxies are shown to be smooth across the boundary before the outbreak, functioning as a placebo-period check that precedes the post-outbreak results.

Spillover diagnostics using two additional conflict datasets test whether messaging affects violence unrelated to the targeted armed group; detailed tables supporting this null-spillover claim are placed only in the online appendix.

Constructs a placebo assignment among comparison taxpayers that mimics the increasing relationship between assignment probability and preperiod size, reruns the main procedure on this placebo treatment, and presents the estimates in an online appendix figure.

The mechanism analysis separately plots the instrument's association with pre-1940 values of the same mechanism variables before turning to post-period effects, treating the pre-period panel as a placebo check.

Reports a separate figure showing dispensing trends for all opioids other than OxyContin around the reformulation date, used as a falsification check that no comparable structural break appears in a drug category the reformulation should not have affected.

Shows year-by-year event-study estimates of the administration treatment effect with confidence bands to visually assess whether treated and comparison taxpayers were on similar trends before the reform, describing the preperiod pattern as flat.

No formal statistical pre-trends test is reported anywhere; pre-treatment fit is instead conveyed only visually, through the top panel of the main comparison figure showing each method's fitted pre-period trend against the raw outcome trajectory.

The mechanism analysis separately plots the instrument's association with pre-1940 values of the same mechanism variables before turning to post-period effects, treating the pre-period panel as a placebo check.

Reports a figure plotting average dispensing before and after the ownership-change event, with confidence intervals, letting readers visually assess the flatness of the pre-period trend for pharmacies that later convert to chain ownership.

Reports a graphical pre-trends check in the main event-study figure and describes a supplementary longer-horizon pre-trends check placed in the online appendix, both offered as support for the parallel-trends assumption.

Reports the first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instrument in the main results table, separately for the pooled sample and for each applicant subgroup, rather than only stating that the first stage is strong.

The first-stage relationship between judge leniency and appeal allowance is shown twice, in a binned local-linear-regression figure and in a regression table across multiple post-decision years and covariate sets.

Reports a first-stage F-statistic for the administration-assignment instrument directly in the text and shows the year-by-year first-stage relationship in a figure with confidence bands.

First-stage F-statistics are reported in the main first-stage table for the full sample and for each of the hidden and transparent subsamples, and the text interprets these as evidence against weak-instrument bias.

A placebo-style check on local political outcomes, such as protests or turnover of village leadership, is reported in an online appendix table and summarized in a footnote as showing no observable treatment-related differences.

A footnote describes a formal statistical test of whether pre-period event-study coefficients differ from each other for each outcome, with outcomes that fail this test routed to a separate sensitivity-bounds analysis detailed in the online appendix.
A specification test targeting the testable inequality implications of the exclusion-type assumption is applied to the experimental data as a diagnostic for the mechanism analysis.

Reports the first-stage F-statistic for the excluded instrument in the main results table, separately for the pooled sample and for each applicant subgroup, rather than only stating that the first stage is strong.

First-stage F-statistics are reported in the main first-stage table for the full sample and for each of the hidden and transparent subsamples, and the text interprets these as evidence against weak-instrument bias.
First-stage F-statistics are reported directly beneath each 2SLS coefficient in the results tables, so instrument strength can be read alongside the corresponding second-stage estimate.

pointers.locator: Sec. I.A; online Appendix Tables B1-B2 (not available)
pointers.statement: Selective attrition between the main experiment and the follow-up call is checked against observable characteristics and against the original sign-up decision, with the supporting tables placed in an online appendix that is outside the scope of this reading.

The text discusses possible sample attrition from reverse migration out of destination commuting zones and argues that the timing of the study cohorts' birth years makes this an unlikely source of bias.

The paper does not describe household-level survey attrition or nonresponse as a design concern, consistent with its repeated cross-sectional (rather than panel) survey structure; this is treated as not applicable rather than analyzed.

Presents a quarter-by-quarter comparison, shown as a figure of point estimates with confidence intervals, of the probability that a parcel is under an active lease across the two mechanisms, to check whether the mechanisms differ systematically in how often a transaction is actually completed.
Match rates between administrative datasets and the census backbone are reported and tested for discontinuity at the population cutoff, and found unrelated to treatment status.

pointers.locator: Section VB, footnote on data construction
pointers.statement: States that attrition from the target experiment sample is not correlated with potential outcomes, citing an online appendix table rather than presenting the underlying attrition regression in the main text.
Reports a manipulation test on the density of the running variable at the cutoff, presented together with a companion density figure in the main text.

pointers.locator: Section IIIA, referencing online Appendix Figure B-4
pointers.statement: Reports a density-continuity test in the spirit of a standard manipulation test for the running variable around the kink threshold, checking continuity of the wage density and its first derivative, with the test itself placed in an online appendix.

pointers.locator: Section III.A, referencing Appendix Figure B2
pointers.statement: A manipulation test on the running variable's density, using the number of properties across the boundary, is run and reported in an appendix figure.

pointers.locator: Section IIIB, footnote referencing appendix figure
pointers.statement: Reports a density-based check for strategic bunching of taxpayers around the assignment margin and states that no bunching is found in either the pre- or post-reform period, with the supporting figure held in the online appendix.

The paper compares the shape of the pooled empirical retirement-age density around statutory ages against the density predicted by the reference-dependence model and by a rival behavioral model, using the presence or absence of missing mass on one side of the threshold as the distinguishing test.

Excess bunching mass at the reference point is quantified against an explicit counterfactual distribution built from potential (rather than realized) gains, with bootstrap-based confidence bands shown directly on the bunching figure, following the bunching-estimator literature.

pointers.locator: Sec. I.A; online Appendix Tables B1-B2 (not available)

A footnote asserts that results are robust to bandwidth choice throughout and points readers to an online appendix for a bandwidth-sweep figure not included in the pages read.

pointers.locator: Section IIIB, footnote referencing appendix figure
pointers.statement: Reports a density-based check for strategic bunching of taxpayers around the assignment margin and states that no bunching is found in either the pre- or post-reform period, with the supporting figure held in the online appendix.

A footnote states that the instrument also does not predict several other baseline socioeconomic characteristics of destination commuting zones, with the supporting table placed in the online appendix.

Finite-sample size and power simulations, including data-generating processes calibrated to the empirical application, are summarized narratively in the main text but reported in full only in the online Appendix, which is not part of the supplied text.

Introduces a placebo estimator, distinct from the standard event-study pretrends test which it argues is invalid under heterogeneous effects, and applies it (with versions lagged two and three periods) to both empirical applications.

A dedicated placebo table regresses the instrument on pre-treatment-period school-attendance and education outcomes across several decades to check for pre-existing trends before the Migration period begins.

Treats the statistical insignificance of the pre-period ownership-change coefficient, reported alongside the main post-period estimate in the same table, as a check on the identifying assumption rather than relying only on the visual figure.

A footnote describes a formal statistical test of whether pre-period event-study coefficients differ from each other for each outcome, with outcomes that fail this test routed to a separate sensitivity-bounds analysis detailed in the online appendix.
Pre-birth coefficients in the single-group, difference-in-differences and triple-difference event studies are presented directly in the main results figure as the primary pre-trend check.

Event-study figures for hospitals, physicians, and infant mortality are placed in the main text as the primary way of checking pre-trends, with the discussion explicitly describing the absence of significant pre-period coefficients as support for the identifying assumption.

Reports two alternative theory-based bandwidth-selection criteria side by side in the nonparametric results table and separately plots the coefficient across a full grid of bandwidths in a dedicated sensitivity figure.

pointers.locator: Section IIIA, referencing online Appendix Figure B-6
pointers.statement: Reports sensitivity of the regression kink point estimates to the choice of bandwidth around the threshold in an online appendix figure.
A footnote asserts that results are robust to bandwidth choice throughout and points readers to an online appendix for a bandwidth-sweep figure not included in the pages read.

A nonparametric figure of price effects against distance to the district capital is estimated with locally weighted regressions using a stated kernel type and bandwidth, functioning as a visual sensitivity check on the linear heterogeneity specification reported in the accompanying table.

pointers.locator: Section IV.E, Robustness to Other RD Specifications
pointers.statement: Robustness to a CER-optimal bandwidth, fixed bandwidths of 100 and 200, a quadratic polynomial, and a uniform kernel is summarized in the main text with the underlying tables placed in the online appendix.

Reports confidence sets under two different rule-of-thumb smoothness-bound choices side by side in the main comparison table, functioning as a form of tuning-parameter sensitivity check for the bandwidth-like curvature bound.
Reports a placebo exercise built by permuting cutoff points across lotteries at random, comparing the true reduced-form coefficient to the resulting distribution of placebo coefficients in a figure.
Uses a policy subperiod during which the schedule kink was removed as a placebo test of the regression kink design, estimating the change in slope in that subperiod.

pointers.locator: Section III.F; Figure 5; Appendix Table B3
pointers.statement: Four alternative catchment boundaries for other, unaffected wells are used as placebo treatment boundaries in the same RD specification, with the figure shown in the main text and coefficients tabulated in an appendix table.

Reports an exogeneity test comparing the reduced-form relationship between the instrument and the long-run outcome inside a state where the film was banned versus all other states, using the ban as a test of the exclusion restriction.

Figure 4 summarizes sixteen placebo estimates from four placebo strategies (other states, noncompliant UP districts, the earlier-census cutoff, split-ineligible villages) against the real RD estimates in one coefficient plot and discusses how many placebos reach conventional significance.

pointers.locator: Section V, Childless and Lower-Income Comparison Groups; Figure 4
pointers.statement: Childless women are assigned placebo birth years drawn from the distribution of actual birth years among never-married mothers, and the same triple-difference specification is applied to this placebo sample as a falsification exercise summarized in a dedicated figure.

The appendix instrumental-variable table reports a first-stage F-statistic and an overidentification test p-value alongside the second-stage estimate for the death-indicator instrument, without discussing either statistic's adequacy in the surrounding text.

pointers.locator: Section III; online Appendix Figure D16
pointers.statement: Two additional instrument constructions are built from alternative sources of origin-county variation, and a formal overidentification test comparing all three versions is reported in the main text, with the full comparison figure placed in the online appendix.

An over-identified version using country-specific shocks is reported in the supplementary appendix together with a shock-level over-identification test p-value, cited as support for the identifying assumptions.
For the structural model, an appendix robustness check calibrates two more parameters so the system is overidentified and reports tests of the overidentifying restrictions.

Before any regression, the paper shows raw mortality time series by region and binned scatterplots of mortality against the percentile of ethnic share, separately for nonfamine years and the famine year, so the reader sees the sign reversal in the raw data.
Binned scatter plots of the industry-level first-stage and reduced-form relationships for the preferred specification are relegated to a supplementary figure mentioned in a footnote.
Before regressions, a binned scatterplot of belief update against potential update is shown separately for treated and control groups, with the difference in slopes interpreted as the learning rate.

Before any regression, the paper shows raw mortality time series by region and binned scatterplots of mortality against the percentile of ethnic share, separately for nonfamine years and the famine year, so the reader sees the sign reversal in the raw data.

Before regressions, descriptive figures show territorial control over time and raw time series of attack rates for treated and other villages, so the reader sees the treatment actually occurred and the raw pattern behind the estimates.
Distributions of prior beliefs are plotted as histograms with the expert forecast marked by a dashed line before treatment effects are presented.

Reports a formal coefficient-stability statistic for selection on unobservables computed from the unmatched and propensity-score-matched samples, alongside balance tables and density plots for the matched samples that are placed in the online appendix.

pointers.locator: Footnote 35; Appendix Tables A7 and A8
pointers.statement: Lee bounds are computed for the long-run outcomes using the short-run attrition gap as the assumed differential attrition, reported in appendix tables and described as conservative.

pointers.locator: Section 3.1 Robustness; footnote 15; Appendix Figure A.1
pointers.statement: A honest-DID style sensitivity analysis reports confidence sets over how far post-period trend violations may exceed pre-period ones; the footnote explains the procedure and cautions that it and the visual pre-trend evidence are formally valid only for binary treatment.

Parallel-trend figures for financial, utilization, readmission, mortality, and satisfaction outcomes are placed in the main text, plotting relative-year coefficients normalized to the exposure year with confidence bands, for both the full sample and the matched sample.

Pre-trends are shown graphically in three event-study figures (semi-decade district estimates, SDID trend plots with pre-period weights, village imputation event study) and a cohort-specific exposure figure; the text reads these visually rather than reporting a formal pre-trend test.

An appendix table characterizes the complier population induced by the instrument, comparing them to the full diagnosed cohort and to all for-profit enrollees, and is summarized narratively in the main text.
Complier characteristics are compared with the analysis sample in an appendix table and used to discuss why OLS and IV differ and whom the LATE covers.
The text-based measure is validated informally by listing well-known brands that rank at the top, by industry breadth, and by reporting its correlation with the vendor-based portfolio.

pointers.statement: Monotonicity is probed indirectly by checking that subgroup-specific first stages are never negative and by re-estimating the leniency instrument on complementary subpopulations, with the underlying estimates placed in an online appendix table and only the qualitative conclusion discussed in the mai

A companion figure showing that the probability of collateralizing declines as the threshold rises, holding losses fixed, is offered in the main text as support for the monotonicity assumption underlying the instrumental-variables interpretation.

pointers.locator: Section IVC, Validity of the Averages
pointers.statement: Tests for intertemporal and intrastation spillovers of the encouragement, presenting the underlying estimates only in an online appendix figure and using the check to justify pooling all assigned team-days.

Possible spillovers onto comparison units are addressed diagnostically in two ways: an appendix matching design that pairs each treated unit only with units from different markets, and a robustness sample restricted to transactions too small to plausibly move market-wide outcomes.

A leave-one-out exercise, described in the main text with results plotted in the appendix, drops sample observations one at a time and reports the resulting distribution of RD point estimates and associated p-values as a check on inference.

pointers.locator: Section 5.1; Appendix Figure A.11, Tables A.25, A.26
pointers.statement: Electoral data reliability is probed by plotting vote distributions and regressing indicators of suspicious support and tallies on programme intensity to check fraud is uncorrelated with treatment.

pointers.statement: A dedicated subsection tests each modelling assumption: homogeneity by achievement via percentile-centred reweighting, additive separability via interactions of scores and choices, no comparative advantage via a rank-order test, and additivity of school effects via chained pairwise comparisons; each

Persistence in the pre-treatment prediction errors is diagnosed by fitting an autoregressive model to the synthetic-control residuals, which the paper treats as an input both to choosing the cross-fitting block count and to calibrating the application-based simulations.

Lower and upper attrition bounds following an established sample-selection bounding method are computed for every follow-up treatment effect and reported as extra rows directly inside the main results table rather than in a separate bounds table.

pointers.locator: Section IVC, "Causal Effect of Education on IQ"
pointers.statement: As an auxiliary diagnostic connecting the instrument to a direct ability measure, the paper reports a separate IV regression of a standardized IQ test score on schooling using the same reform instrument, with the estimates placed in the online appendix.

A separate balance check compares HD and LD sections on non-work interaction, temperature, and noise to rule these out as confounding physical-environment differences, reported in an online appendix table.
The text notes that random assignment of the instrument can in principle be verified with usual balance tests, but no balance table for the empirical application is presented in the main text.

Structural break estimates are illustrated by overlaying piecewise linear trend fits on cumulative daily accounts within each regime, following a cited AER paper's visual approach.

Excess bunching mass at the reference point is quantified against an explicit counterfactual distribution built from potential (rather than realized) gains, with bootstrap-based confidence bands shown directly on the bunching figure, following the bunching-estimator literature.

A calibration exercise compares estimated race probabilities against self-reported race in the matched validation sample, checking whether predicted probabilities track the 45-degree line, and repeats the check separately for EITC claimants and nonclaimants.

A footnote reports a fertility and maternal-mortality check meant to rule out that the number of births used both as the mortality-rate denominator and as regression weights is itself confounded by treatment.

pointers.locator: Section 6.2 and 6.3, references to Supplementary Appendix C
pointers.statement: For both applications, the reported robust confidence sets are compared with the sample analogue of the identified set in the supplementary appendix, to separate the roles of sampling uncertainty and identified-set length.
A separate comparison sample of eligible non-participants from the same regions is described and used to characterize how the experimental sample differs from the broader population on observables.

Reports in an appendix table that loan noncompliance is uncorrelated with treatment-group assignment and orthogonal to a range of baseline socioeconomic characteristics, supporting the validity of the instrument used for the LATE specifications.

pointers.locator: Section I.C Randomization Process and Compliance
pointers.statement: The paper reports a compliance diagnostic showing that assignment to the 2018 versus 2019 conversion wave was followed almost exactly, with only a small number of control districts converting ahead of schedule.

pointers.locator: Section IVA, online Appendix Figure A4
pointers.statement: The paper decomposes LATE estimates into potential outcomes of compliers under allowance versus denial, a diagnostic-like exercise placed in the online appendix and only summarized narratively in the main text.

Compositional selection of new hires is checked by predicting an above-average wage indicator from CPS demographics and using that prediction as the outcome in a staggered DiD; the coefficient is reported only in a footnote.

A knowledge-check question after each video documents comprehension across arms (appendix figure), and rewatch take-up of the reminder link is disclosed in a footnote; the appendix is also cited for evidence that participants engaged with the material as expected.

A joint F-test of whether the transparent-IV experience profile is flat, and a parallel test for the hidden-IV profile, are reported in a footnote as a formal check of the model's constant-returns-to-skill assumption.

Each extracted culture type is validated by regressing an established external marker (ESG scores, Glassdoor ratings, patents, R&D, restatements, volatility, ROA, sales growth) on the type-specific tone, with the sign pattern read as construct validity.

Before interpreting the intermediary variable's incremental predictive power, the paper reports that the composite risk-premium control is itself a statistically robust predictor across all portfolios, used as an internal check that the control is a meaningful benchmark rather than a weak placebo.
Pearson correlation matrices for the regression samples are placed in the Internet Appendix and cited as a check that multicollinearity is unlikely.

pointers.locator: Section V.B; results tabulated in the online appendix
pointers.statement: A formal test of the sign of the key bias-determining covariance terms from the paper's bias proposition is reported, estimated separately by race and by predicted-race percentile and aggregated by population share, rejecting a one-sided null in the hypothesized direction.

Coverage of nominal confidence intervals is reported as the paper's primary diagnostic of inference quality, computed by simulation for each variance-estimation method and each estimator/design combination, rather than relying on the asymptotic theorem alone.

Validates the reliability of independently collected data branches by reporting, in footnotes, that station-level revenue and escort figures from two separate station-side branches correlate strongly with each other and with an independent street-level branch.

The paper's central diagnostic is its own nonparametric test of the exclusion and monotonicity assumptions, reported as a test statistic and p-value under four alternative maximum-treatment-effect bounds.

An empirical Monte Carlo study calibrated to resemble the experimental data is used to check the bias and coverage properties of the proposed inference procedure before it is applied to the real results.

As a look-ahead check, firm, person and product names are masked with spaCy in a random subsample and tone agreement between masked and unmasked text is reported as evidence the model is not exploiting entity identities.
Out-of-state migration is checked with an external survey (ACS) at county level around events, using raw plots and an event-study specification, reported in an appendix.

pointers.locator: Section IVC, Validity of the Averages
pointers.statement: Cross-checks the descriptive sample's revenue and quota estimates against independently collected pre-study qualitative proxies and against agents' self-reported income from a post-study exit survey as an informal external validity check.

The comparison of subgroup treatment-effect differences estimated in-sample versus in a held-out sample is used as the paper's central diagnostic for whether the predicted heterogeneity reflects a genuine pattern rather than overfitting.

Joint continuity of a large set of pre-election covariates at the cutoff is tested with the Canay and Kamat (2017) permutation test, for the full sample and several subsamples, reported in an appendix table.

Reports a check of whether treatment effects on investment fade in the second year among households already flooded in the first year, pointing to an appendix table and summarizing the result as no evidence of fading.
